title: Why U.S. Borrowing Costs Keep Climbing Despite Treasury’s Efforts | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Four CFR experts explain why Treasury's yen-support and buyback interventions failed to lower long-term US yields, with the 30-year at 5.36 percent, and cite fundamentals, AI capex of about 1.8 percent of GDP and Brent above $110 as drivers spreading globally.

insights.claim: The 30-year US Treasury yield hit a nineteen-year high of 5.36 percent, prompting Bessent to try a coordinated yen intervention and expanded long-bond buybacks.
insights.speaker: Benn Steil
insights.so_what: Long-end yields are at multi-decade highs despite official efforts.
insights.locator: Treasury Market Ploys Won’t Lower U.S. Borrowing Costs

insights.claim: The July 31 US-Japan yen intervention lifted the yen from 164 to 155 per dollar, but Japan spent about $99 billion while its foreign-securities reserves fell about $88 billion, suggesting it sold Treasuries rather than using the FIMA repo facility.
insights.speaker: Benn Steil
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: Japan's yen defense can add selling pressure on Treasuries.

insights.claim: Treasury's September 10 buyback of $5.2 billion was only 0.016 percent of the marketable Treasury market and failed to lower rates, and the August 19 doubling announcement only briefly pushed yields down.
insights.speaker: Benn Steil
insights.so_what: Buybacks at this scale do not move long rates; fade announcement rallies.

insights.claim: Only fundamental changes in supply and demand for US debt, such as lower deficits, lower inflation, lower AI infrastructure borrowing and less aggressive sanctions that encourage de-dollarization, can durably lower rates, and none appear imminent.
insights.speaker: Benn Steil
insights.so_what: Ad hoc gimmicks burn credibility; term premium stays elevated.
insights.quote: Ad hoc government gimmickry merely burns credibility.
insights.locator: What can we conclude from these two failed interventions?

insights.claim: Yields have risen despite Treasury actions because fundamentals overpower them: resilient growth, high inflation, tightening monetary policy and bond supply outpacing demand.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Patterson
insights.so_what: Direction of yields remains biased higher absent fundamental change.

insights.claim: Contagion from US yields varies: Mexico's bonds closely track US peers, Brazil's are dominated by its election, and France and the UK also face domestic deficit and bond supply concerns.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Patterson

insights.claim: Goldman estimates US AI-related capex at $581 billion this year, 1.8 percent of GDP, rising to 2.8 percent by 2028, with about $1 trillion globally.

insights.so_what: AI capex is a material source of capital demand.

insights.claim: Each additional 1 percent of GDP in borrowing raises long-term borrowing costs by 20-30 basis points, so AI spending probably lifts the 10-year yield by a bit more than that, smaller than the effect of a budget deficit near 6 percent of GDP.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: AI capex adds a few tens of basis points to term yields; the deficit matters more.

insights.claim: Higher yields could stress tech firms by making data center and energy financing costlier and raising bubble-pop odds, though the 1994 bond meltdown coincided with the start of a six-year internet stock bull run.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: The link between high rates and tech distress is uncertain.

insights.claim: Brent rose from about $70 a barrel in early July to above $110, often in lockstep with interest rates, with an even sharper rise in diesel.

insights.so_what: Oil is a common global driver of the rate sell-off.
